Peeters, Elke, Vanacker, Peter, Woodhall, Mark et al. Supranuclear gaze palsy in glycine receptor antibody-positive progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus. Movement disorders : official journal of the Movement Disorder Society. 2012;27(14):1830-2.

Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM) is a subacute, potentially life-threatening disorder with rigidity, painful spasms, brainstem signs (including brainstem myoclonicus), and dysautonomia. 1 Most PERM patients have anti glutamic acid decarboxylase (GAD) antibodies (Abs). 1 Recently, several PERM cases with glycine receptor (GlyR) Abs have been reported on. 2–7 Here, we present a GlyR Ab-positive PERM patient with supranuclear upward gaze palsy and slow saccades. On December 1, 2011, a 37-year-old man was referred with a 1-month-history of muscle jerks, painful spasms, falls, diplopia, dysphagia, incomplete jaw opening, constipation, urinary retention, and pruritus of the arms and back. On examination (see Video), he was well oriented and had trismus, marked rigidity of the ankles and axial muscles, generalized hyperreflexia, bilateral Babinski signs, generalized myoclonic jerks elicited by sudden noise or touch, and prominent supranuclear upward gaze restriction. Downward and horizontal gaze were unrestricted. Upward saccades were severely slowed, whereas downward and horizontal saccades were mildly slowed. He had been hospitalized elsewhere 9 and 7 months before because of similar episodes, which had resolved almost completely with temporary corticosteroid treatment. His medical history was otherwise unremarkable. Laboratory testing on admission showed leukocytosis (17, 000 /C2 10 6/L) and elevated C-reactive protein (125. 4 mg/L) and creatine kinase (656 U/L). Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) analysis showed mild lymphocytic pleocytosis (6. 4 cells/mL) and seven oligoclonal bands. Paravertebral needle electromyography (EMG) showed continuous motor-unit activity, despite attempted relaxation. Surface EMG during jerks was consistent with brainstem myoclonus (Fig. 1). Brain and spinal MRI and whole-body F-18 fluorodeoxyglucose-PET/CT were normal. Abs to GAD, a m p h i p h y s i n , Y o , H u , R i , C V 2 , M a 2 , N M D A r e c e p t o r s , voltage-gated potassium and calcium channels were negative in serum, but GlyR Abs were strongly positive in serum and CSF. Diazepam and baclofen were started and relieved the spasms and jerks. He received plasma exchange from December 6 to December 16. Intravenous methylprednisolone (500 mg daily for 5 days) was started on December 22, followed by oral therapy (tapering over 4 months from 96 mg daily to 8 mg on alternate days). His condition markedly improved in January 2012. Upon discharge on January 21, neurological exam was normal, apart from mild hypertonia of the limbs and slightly slowed upward saccades (see Video). Bladder voiding remained difficult, necessitating intermittent self-catheterization. So far, 8 patients with GlyR Abs have been reported on, each of whom had a clinical picture of PERM. 2–7 Most of these patients had ocular motility problems, including diplopia, 3, 4, 6 impaired smooth pursuit, 4, 5 unilateral abducens palsy, 6 internuclear ophthalmoplegia, 4 gaze-evoked rotary nystagmus, 7 and slow horizontal saccades. 7 Two patients had horizontal gaze palsies that were not overcome with the doll’s eye maneuver, indicating that the palsy was not supranuclear. 2, 7 Our present GlyR Ab-positive PERM case is the first with a supranuclear gaze palsy and slow vertical saccades, suggesting involvement of the rostral midbrain and thus extending the apparent anatomical distribution of the effects of GlyR Abs. Our patient responded well to corticosteroids, but tended to relapse after corticosteroid discontinuation. The course of GlyR Ab-positive PERM is variable, ranging from relapsing/remitting 2, 4, 6, 7 to monophasic. 3, 6 It remains to be established which immunotherapeutic regimen is most effective against PERM.
